title: Planning a Uganda Photography Tour for Your Camera Club? Start With the Gorilla Permits
meta_title: Uganda Photography Tour Planning for a Camera Club
meta_description: Plan a Uganda photography tour for your club: gorillas, chimps, Murchison Falls, best months, vehicles and group costs, from our Nairobi team.
excerpt: A Uganda photography tour gives a camera club gorillas, chimpanzees, Murchison Falls and the Kazinga Channel in one 9-11 day loop. Here is how to plan the route, seasons, vehicles and permits as a group.
content:
A Uganda photography tour for a camera club combines three kinds of shooting in one trip: mountain gorillas in Bwindi, chimpanzees in Kibale, and savannah and river scenes at Murchison Falls and Queen Elizabeth. Plan 9 to 11 days, book gorilla permits early and travel in the drier months for the easiest conditions.

Organising a trip for a photographic society is harder than booking a safari for two. Members want window seats, time at sunrise, room for long lenses and a guide who understands why the vehicle must stop and wait. This guide covers routes, rules, seasons and costs from the organiser's side, and our club and society safaris page shows how we build these trips around a group.

Quick Facts

  • Ideal length: 9-11 days for a Uganda photography tour that covers forest and savannah
  • Signature subjects: Mountain gorillas, chimpanzees, Murchison Falls, Kazinga Channel wildlife, shoebill
  • Gorilla permit: US$800 per foreign non-resident (Uganda Wildlife Authority, checked November 2026)
  • Gorilla rules: Up to 8 visitors per gorilla family, one hour with them, no flash, minimum age 15
  • Driest months: December-February and June-August
  • Best group size: 8-16 photographers, travelling about four to a pop-up roof vehicle

What Does a Uganda Photography Tour for a Club Cover?

A Uganda photography tour covers more variety than most single-country safaris: primates in rainforest, big rivers, open savannah and wetland birds. The usual loop runs from Entebbe to Murchison Falls in the north, south to Kibale and Queen Elizabeth, then to Bwindi in the far south-west.

That variety is the reason clubs pick a Uganda photography tour over a pure savannah destination. In one trip a member can practise slow-shutter water work at the falls, low-light portraits in the forest, telephoto birds from a boat and classic game-drive frames of elephants, buffalo and lions. Few itineraries give a portfolio that range in under two weeks.

A Uganda photography tour also suits clubs because the days have a natural rhythm. Gorilla and chimp treks fill mornings, boat trips and drives fill afternoons, and evenings are free for image reviews. Our guide to the best national parks in Uganda explains each park in more depth if your committee wants background before choosing.

Who should join a Uganda photography tour?

A Uganda photography tour fits members who can walk several hours on steep, muddy ground and who are happy to trade some comfort for subjects. Beginners do well because guides find the animals, while experienced shooters get rare chances such as gorillas in dappled light and the shoebill at close range.

When Is the Best Light for Photographing Uganda?

The best light for photographing Uganda comes in the two drier seasons, December to February and June to August. Skies are clearer, trails are firmer and the savannah grass is shorter, which makes animals easier to frame. The wetter months give lush greens and dramatic skies, but rain can cut a shooting day short.

Uganda sits on the equator, so sunrise and sunset fall at roughly the same time all year, close to 07:00 and 19:00 local time. Golden light is short. On a Uganda photography tour, plan game drives to leave camp before sunrise and return after sunset where park rules allow, and keep midday for travel, downloads and rest.

MonthsConditionsWhat it means for photographers
December-FebruaryDrier, warm, some haze late in the seasonEasiest gorilla treks; good savannah work; book permits early
March-MayLong rains, heaviest in AprilGreen forest, few visitors, frequent downpours; lower-season permit offers possible
June-AugustDrier, cooler morningsClear light, firm trails, peak demand for permits and lodges
September-NovemberShort rains buildDramatic skies and fresh green; expect wet afternoons and muddy trails

Rain does not stop a gorilla trek, and some photographers like the soft, even light of an overcast forest. What rain changes is comfort and gear risk, so a Uganda photography tour in the wetter months needs rain covers, dry bags and spare time in the itinerary.

How Do Gorilla and Chimpanzee Rules Shape What Your Club Can Shoot?

Primate rules in Uganda limit group size, time and distance, and they are the single biggest factor in planning a Uganda photography tour. Each habituated gorilla family takes up to eight visitors a day for one hour, so a club of 16 is split across at least two families, and sometimes across different sectors of Bwindi.

Gorilla trekking in Bwindi

Gorilla trekking in Bwindi starts with a briefing at the sector office, then a hike that can take from under an hour to most of the day, depending on where the family slept. Flash is forbidden, visitors keep about seven metres away, and the hour starts once the group reaches the gorillas. Read our Bwindi gorilla trekking guide for sectors and fitness.

On a Uganda photography tour, the gorilla hour feels short. Agree a simple routine as a club: phones away, one camera body with a mid-range zoom ready before the final approach, and no jostling for the front. Rangers move the group around so that everyone gets a clear view, and calm groups often get the best positions.

The habituation experience for serious shooters

The gorilla habituation experience in Bwindi's Rushaga sector lets a small group spend up to four hours with a family still getting used to people. Places are few and cost more than a standard permit, but on a Uganda photography tour with keen shooters the extra time is valuable. Our post on gorilla trekking vs habituation sets out the trade-offs.

Chimpanzees in Kibale

Chimpanzee tracking in Kibale is faster-moving than gorilla work. Chimps travel through the canopy and down to the ground, so photographers need high ISO and patience with branches in the frame. Morning and afternoon sessions are offered, and the Kibale chimpanzee trekking guide covers timings and age limits.

Where Are the Best Savannah and Water Shots in Uganda?

The best savannah and water shots in Uganda come from Murchison Falls National Park and Queen Elizabeth National Park. Murchison gives the falls, the Nile and big herds of Uganda kob, giraffe and buffalo, while Queen Elizabeth adds the Kazinga Channel boat trip and the open plains of Ishasha.

Murchison Falls and the Nile

Murchison Falls is where the Nile forces its way through a narrow gorge before dropping into the river below. The hike to the top of the falls is the strongest landscape session of any Uganda photography tour, ideally in late afternoon, and the boat trip upstream towards the base gives hippos, crocodiles, elephants at the water's edge and riverside birds.

The northern bank of the park holds the main game-drive circuit, with Rothschild's giraffe, kob, buffalo, elephants and a chance of lions. Ziwa Rhino Sanctuary, on the road from Kampala, adds rhino tracking on foot, a subject Uganda's parks no longer have in the wild.

Queen Elizabeth and the Kazinga Channel

Queen Elizabeth National Park suits telephoto work from the water. The afternoon launch on the Kazinga Channel, which links Lake George and Lake Edward, passes hippos, buffalo, elephants and huge numbers of waterbirds. In the southern Ishasha sector, guides search fig trees for lions resting in the branches. Our 4-day Queen Elizabeth National Park trip shows how the park fits into a short loop.

Which Route Works Best for a Club of Photographers?

The route that works best for a photography club is a 9- to 11-day loop from Entebbe: Murchison Falls, Kibale, Queen Elizabeth and Bwindi, with two nights at each main stop. Two nights per place give one full shooting day and a second chance if weather or animals do not cooperate.

DaysLocationMain photography
1EntebbeArrival; optional shoebill canoe trip in Mabamba Swamp if flights allow
2-3Ziwa, then Murchison FallsRhino tracking on foot, top of the falls, Nile boat trip, northern bank drives
4-5KibaleChimpanzee tracking, Bigodi wetland walk for birds and monkeys
6-7Queen ElizabethKazinga Channel launch, crater lakes, game drives
8-9BwindiGorilla trekking; optional second trek or habituation
10EntebbeDomestic flight or long drive back, departure

Drive times are long on a Uganda photography tour. Kampala to Murchison takes most of a day with the Ziwa stop, Murchison to Kibale is another full day, and the road from Bwindi back to Entebbe can take 9 to 10 hours, which is why many clubs fly out from the airstrips near Bwindi. Our 9 day Uganda gorilla safari for clubs follows this loop and can be reshaped for photographers.

Should the club add a second gorilla day?

A second gorilla day is the upgrade most photographers value on a Uganda photography tour, because the first trek often goes to adrenaline. The cost is a second permit per person and an extra night, so offer it as an option to keen members rather than building it into everyone's price.

Vehicles, Boats and Camera Gear for a Group

Vehicles decide whether a Uganda photography tour succeeds. A Uganda safari vehicle with a pop-up roof normally takes six or seven passengers, but for photographers we suggest about four per vehicle, so each person has a window and space for a bag. It costs more per head, and it is the right call for a camera club.

Boat trips in Murchison and on the Kazinga Channel are usually shared launches on a standard Uganda photography tour. Larger clubs can ask about a private boat for better positioning, and we check what is available for your dates. Sit on the side facing the bank you expect the action on, and keep a lens of at least 300 mm for birds and crocodiles.

What camera kit should members pack?

The ideal kit for a Uganda photography tour is two bodies, a 24-105 mm or 70-200 mm zoom for the forest, and a 100-400 mm or longer lens for savannah and birds. Add a rain cover, dry bags, cleaning cloths and spare batteries, because charging can be limited in forest lodges. Our gorilla trekking packing list covers boots, gloves and rain gear.

Leave the tripod for the falls and the lodge; it is impractical on a gorilla trek. Porters can be hired at the trailhead to carry camera bags. Drones need separate clearance from the Uganda Civil Aviation Authority and Uganda Wildlife Authority, so we advise members not to bring them. Commercial filming in parks also needs its own UWA permission.

How Is a Uganda Photography Tour Priced for a Group?

A Uganda photography tour for a group is priced from four building blocks: permits and park fees per person, lodges per room, vehicles and guides per vehicle, and domestic flights per seat. Group size helps on vehicles and guides, while permits and park entry stay the same per head however many travel.

Cost itemHow it is chargedEffect of a bigger group
Gorilla permitUS$800 per foreign non-resident trekker (checked November 2026)No saving; one permit per person
Chimp permit and park entryPer person, per activity or per 24 hoursNo saving; paid per head
Vehicle and driver-guidePer vehicle per dayShared across four photographers per vehicle
LodgesPer room, by season and standardTwin sharing keeps costs down; singles pay a supplement
Domestic flightsPer seat, with baggage limitsOptional; saves a long road day

Our group terms help a club. For every six paying travellers the seventh place is free, which most clubs give to the trip leader. Members can pay separately and fly in on different flights, a deposit of 30 to 40% holds the booking and the balance is due 2 to 4 weeks before travel. The guide to organising a group safari explains rooming lists and payments, and our group safaris page lists every type of group we plan for.

For any Uganda photography tour, book gorilla permits as early as you can, ideally six months or more ahead for June to August and December to February. Uganda's tourist eVisa is US$50 for a single entry (checked November 2026); members apply online themselves. Our group gorilla trekking in Uganda post explains how permits are spread across families for larger parties.

Insider Tips

  • Split the gorilla days: Put half the club on each family and swap notes over dinner rather than chasing one permit date for everyone
  • Shoot the approach: Set ISO and exposure before the last few metres; the first minutes with the gorillas move fast
  • Keep gear dry: Pack every lens in a dry bag inside the camera bag; forest rain arrives without warning
  • Back up nightly: Bring two portable drives and copy cards every evening, as lodge power can be limited
  • Agree vehicle rotation: Swap seats daily so every member gets time at the front and the best roof hatch
  • Plan a review evening: Book a quiet room at one lodge for a club slide show; ask us when you request a quote

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days does a Uganda photography tour need?

A Uganda photography tour for a club works best over 9 to 11 days. That allows two nights each in Murchison Falls, Kibale, Queen Elizabeth and Bwindi, so every location gets at least one full shooting day. Shorter trips are possible, but the long drives between parks then eat into the morning and evening light that photographers travel for.

Can I use flash when photographing gorillas in Uganda?

No. Flash photography is not allowed with mountain gorillas in Uganda, and the same applies to chimpanzees in Kibale. Photographers need a fast lens and a camera that handles high ISO well, because the forest is dark. Rangers also ask visitors to keep about seven metres from the gorillas and to stay with the group for the one hour allowed.

How much is a gorilla permit for a photography group in Uganda?

A gorilla tracking permit in Uganda costs US$800 per foreign non-resident (checked November 2026), and every member who treks needs one. Uganda Wildlife Authority has offered lower low-season rates in some months, such as April, May and November. Prices change with each tariff, so confirm the rate for your travel dates before you set the club's budget.

Can our camera club fly a drone in Uganda's national parks?

A camera club should not plan on flying drones in Uganda's national parks. Drone flights need clearance from the Uganda Civil Aviation Authority and written permission from Uganda Wildlife Authority for any protected area, and permission for tourists is rarely practical. Members who bring one risk having it held at the airport, so we advise leaving drones at home.

What is the best month for a Uganda photography tour?

The best months for a Uganda photography tour are December to February and June to August, the two drier seasons, when forest trails are firmer and savannah tracks stay open. Wetter months such as April, May and November bring greener scenery, softer light and fewer visitors, but expect rain on most days and muddier gorilla treks.

Final Thoughts

A Uganda photography tour gives a camera club gorillas, chimpanzees, a thundering waterfall and savannah wildlife in one loop, which few other trips can match. Plan for the drier months, two nights per stop and no more than four photographers per vehicle, and secure gorilla permits before anything else.
